base_text: NA27 (= NA28 in Luke), checked against the page images

witnesses.evidence: "Adlegit et alios septuaginta apostolos super duodecim."
"hi autem in civitates mittebantur".

records.wording: NA27 has no καί before ἑτέρους (SBLGNT has it — checked on the page image). Marcionite reading adopted: "seventy" without NA27's bracketed [δύο] ("seventy-two"). Tertullian has septuaginta and builds his comparison on the seventy palm trees of Elim (Exod 15:27); Roth: "Tertullian here attests the former [seventy] as Marcion's reading" (rated very likely). A Marcion witness lacks the bracketed word, so it is not printed (METHOD §5.7). NA27 apparatus for the omission: ℵ A C L W Θ Ξ Ψ f1.13 𝔐 f q sy(s).p bo; Irlat Cl Or. The second bracketed [δύο] ("two by two") is not attested either way and is printed.

witnesses.evidence: "Etiam calciamenta portare vetuit illos… Neminem, inquit, per viam salutaveritis."

records.wording: NA27. Tertullian also says Christ forbade the disciples "even a staff" (4.24.1, nec virgam); no Greek manuscript has a staff in this verse, and Roth takes it from the mission of the twelve (9:3), brought in to match Elisha's staff (2 Kgs 4:29, quoted in 4.24.3).

witnesses.evidence: "Sic et dominus, in quam introissent domum, pacem ei dicere."

records.reason: Inside the attested paragraph 10:1–12. NA27 reads ἐκεῖ ᾖ and μή γε (SBLGNT ᾖ ἐκεῖ, μήγε — checked on the page image).

witnesses.evidence: "Dignus autem operarius mercede sua" (Moreschini; Evans: "Dignus est autem…"), read as the Creator's own rule (Deut 25:4).
"in salutem scilicet eorum qui annuntiationem eius recepissent" — an allusion to those who welcome them (δέχωνται).
"Regnum dei… dum illud iubet annuntiari appropinquasse."

records.wording: NA27. Tertullian's report is indirect and does not show whether ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ("to you") stood in this verse.

witnesses.evidence: "Etiam adicit, ut eis qui illos non recepissent dicerent…"
"Scitote tamen appropinquasse regnum dei… Sic et pulverem iubet excuti in illos in testificationem."

records.wording: NA27, which reads ἤγγικεν without ἐφ' ὑμᾶς and cites Tertullian's Marcion for that text (McionT). "Shake off" (excuti) and "for a testimony" come from the mission of the twelve (9:5); Roth does not count them for this verse.

records.reason: Sodom on that day (10:12) and the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum (10:13–15). Tertullian's commentary is continuous here (4.24.7 on 10:11, 4.24.8 on 10:16). At 10:11 he argues that the command must carry a threat of judgement, "or he commands it in vain", and that the testimony "portends threats" (4.24.7–8). A saying that names the judgement on Sodom, the Creator's own, and a series of woes would have been his proof; he infers the threat instead. In 4.27.1 he counts Christ's "woe" as a mark of the Creator. 10:12 closes the NA27 paragraph 10:1–12; 10:13–15 form a paragraph of their own.

witnesses.evidence: "Qui vos spernit, me spernit."

records.reason: Inside the attested paragraph 10:17–20. NA27 brackets [δύο] here as at 10:1; the attested number at 10:1 is seventy, and the bracketed word is not printed here either.

"I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven." At 10:19 Tertullian explains the snakes and scorpions as spiritual powers whose prince the Creator calls serpent and dragon, and quotes Ps 91:13 and Isa 27:1 for Christ's victory over him (4.24.10). A saying of Jesus describing the fall of Satan from heaven, the image of Isa 14:12, would have served that argument better than the texts he brings in. Its citation by Marinus in the Dialogue of Adamantius (134,5–6) is not evidence for Marcion's text (Roth).

witnesses.evidence: "Quis nunc dabit potestatem calcandi super colubros et scorpios?"
"tunc et scorpios et serpentes sanctis suis subdidit".
»εὐχαριστῶ σοι, κύριε τοῦ οὐρανοῦ«. οὐκ εἶχεν δὲ »καὶ τῆς γῆς«, οὔτε »πάτερ« εἶχεν. ἐλέγχεται δέ· κάτω γὰρ εἶχεν »ναί, ὁ πατήρ«.
"Gratias enim, inquit, ago, et confiteor, domine caeli, quod ea quae erant abscondita sapientibus et prudentibus, revelaveris parvulis."
"Sed in destructionem, inquis, uti traduceret eas" — the Marcionite reading of the verse, which requires that the God who reveals is not said to have hidden.

records.wording: Marcionite readings adopted. (1) εὐχαριστῶ σοι for ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι: both witnesses (gratias ago; Roth: very likely). Tertullian's added "et confiteor" is in his text only and is not adopted (Roth: probable). (2) No vocative πάτερ: Epiphanius states the absence, and Tertullian's quotation lacks it (METHOD §5.3). καὶ τῆς γῆς: Epiphanius states that it was absent too, and Tertullian's quotation lacks it (NA27 apparatus: om. 𝔓45; McionT,E); the words are printed by method (METHOD §11): the correspondential reading marks the omission as a strain that separates the Lord from the earth where the revealing happens, and NA27 continues the line (docs/research/correspondence/word_by_word.md, chapter 8; second_pass.md §3). (3) "What was hidden from the wise and understanding you have revealed to little children": Tertullian's Latin has one verb of hiding, impersonal (ea quae erant abscondita), and cannot render NA27's "you hid these things… and revealed them". His reply in 4.25.6 answers a Marcionite reading that depends on God not being the subject of the hiding. The Greek printed is Roth's retroversion (after Harnack), rated very likely; the exact Greek words are not attested. (4) "Yes, Father" is attested by Epiphanius; the closing clause is not cited and is printed in the NA27 wording. NA27's opening, with [ἐν] τῷ πνεύματι (SBLGNT without ἐν), is printed.

witnesses.evidence: "Omnia sibi tradita dicit a patre."
"Sed, Nemo scit qui sit pater, nisi filius, et qui sit filius, nisi pater, et cuicunque filius revelaverit. Atque ita Christus ignotum deum praedicavit."

records.wording: Marcionite reading adopted: the Father named first ("who the Father is except the son, and who the son is except the Father"; Roth: very likely). Tertullian's quotation has this order; the words in brackets that follow it in the manuscripts of 4.25.10 are a copyist's addition from Matthew 11:27 (Roth, after Braun and the editors). Tertullian's "a patre" lacks μου ("my"); NA27 cites McionT for the omission with D a c l vgww sys. One witness, and Tertullian also writes "the Father" in Prax. 24.5; μου is printed. The present tense γινώσκει is confirmed by Tertullian's scit.

witnesses.evidence: "Beati oculi qui vident quae videtis".
"dico enim vobis, quia prophetae non viderunt quae vos videtis".

records.wording: NA27. Tertullian's quotation is shorter: "the prophets did not see what you see", without "many", "and kings", "wanted to see" and the clause on hearing. NA27 cites McionT with D and the Old Latin for the omission of "and kings". One witness, which may abridge (Roth: possible only); NA27 printed and the evidence noted.
records.western: Without καὶ βασιλεῖς: D it with Tertullian's Marcion.

witnesses.evidence: "In evangelio veritatis legis doctor dominum aggressus, Quid faciens, inquit, vitam aeternam consequar? In haeretico vita solummodo posita est, sine aeternae mentione."
"Viderit nunc si aeternam nostri addiderunt."
εἶπεν τῷ νομικῷ… (the lawyer's question is presupposed).

records.wording: Marcionite reading adopted: ζωήν without αἰώνιον. Tertullian states it as a difference between the two texts ("in the heretical gospel only 'life' is set down, with no mention of 'eternal'"), and in 4.25.18 allows that his own side may have added the word. Roth: very likely. Tertullian does not quote "Teacher" (D also lacks it); one witness, printed.

witnesses.evidence: εἶπεν τῷ νομικῷ »ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τί γέγραπται;«
"Diliges dominum deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua et totis viribus tuis".

records.wording: NA27. Tertullian quotes three clauses (heart, soul, strength) and not the clause on the mind or the neighbour. NA27 cites McionT with D and the Old Latin for the omission of "and with all your mind". Tertullian's three clauses are those of Deut 6:5, which he quotes in that form in 4.27.4, so the shorter form may be his. One witness; NA27 printed and the evidence noted.
records.western: Without "and with all your mind": D it with Tertullian's Marcion.

witnesses.evidence: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς μετὰ τὴν ἀπόκρισιν τοῦ νομικοῦ εἶπεν »ὀρθῶς εἶπες, τοῦτο ποίει, καὶ ζήσῃ«.

records.wording: NA27. Epiphanius has εἶπες ("you have said") for ἀπεκρίθης ("you have answered"); Roth: possible only. Not adopted.

records.reason: The parable of the Samaritan. In both witnesses the exchange with the lawyer closes at 10:28: Epiphanius' sch. 23 ends with "do this and you will live" and sch. 24 is on 11:5; Tertullian passes from 10:28 (4.25.14–18) to 11:1 (4.26.1). Tertullian's aim in 4.25.14–18 is to show that Christ taught the "head of the law" of the Creator; a parable expounding the law's own command (Lev 19:18), with a priest and a Levite in it, would have been his best evidence, and any Marcionite use of it against the Creator's cult would have drawn an answer. Neither witness has the neighbour clause of 10:27, which the parable explains. NA27 begins a new paragraph at 10:29.

Martha and Mary. A separate NA27 paragraph with no attested verse (METHOD §4.3). Neither witness mentions it: Tertullian passes from 10:28 to 11:1, Epiphanius from 10:28 to 11:5. Nothing in the passage bears on Tertullian's or Epiphanius' arguments, so their silence does not show absence; the class is "undetermined", not "attested absent".
